criteria.descriptor: Correctly distinguishes independence/demographic parity, separation/equalized odds, and sufficiency/calibration; correctly states the calibration-vs-equalized-odds impossibility under unequal base rates; and accurately explains the base-rate mechanism (the PPV/FPR/FNR-prevalence linkage). Full marks require no false claims (e.g., not asserting both can be jointly achieved by a non-perfect model, not misdefining the metrics).

Covers: (a) why the two audit findings are consistent, (b) the impossibility/mechanism, (c) that retraining cannot satisfy both, (d) a chosen governing criterion with a remediation path, and (e) at least one of label-bias scrutiny, evaluation rigor (CIs/subgroups/monitoring), or the legal constraint. Deduct for omitted dimensions.

Justifies the recommended fairness criterion using the concrete harm/error asymmetry rather than asserting it, explains why the naive 'fix both' request fails, and reasons about the legal/deployment tension of group-conditional thresholds instead of proposing them uncritically.

Explanation is well structured and uses fairness vocabulary precisely (calibration, PPV, FPR/FNR, equalized odds, base rate), and clearly frames fairness as an explicit value choice with a stated trade-off suitable for a stakeholder design review.

expected_answer_points: Names the fairness families precisely and maps the audit: calibration/sufficiency holds while equalized-odds/separation (equal FPR) is violated.
States the impossibility result: calibration and equalized odds cannot both hold when group base rates differ, except for a perfect classifier (Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan / Chouldechova).
Explains the mechanism -- PPV, FPR, and FNR are algebraically tied to prevalence (ideally the identity FPR = (p/(1-p)).((1-PPV)/PPV).(1-FNR)) -- so the two findings are consistent, not a defect.
Concludes that 'just retrain / add data / tune thresholds' cannot satisfy both objectives; those only move the model along the trade-off, never off it.
Selects a governing fairness criterion justified by the specific harm asymmetry (denying creditworthy applicants argues for error-rate balance) and frames the choice as a documented value decision.
Names post-processing (Hardt et al. group-specific thresholds) but flags the disparate-treatment / fair-lending (ECOA/Reg B) legal tension of race-conditional decision rules.

Adds rigor: questions whether the label is a biased proxy, reports subgroup/intersectional metrics with confidence intervals and adequate sample sizes, monitors under distribution shift, and communicates the trade-off transparently.
common_pitfalls: Treats the FPR disparity as a straightforward bug to be 'debugged out,' not recognizing it is the mathematical consequence of equal calibration plus unequal base rates.
Claims both calibration and equalized odds can be achieved with a better model, more data, or threshold tuning -- missing that only a perfect classifier or equal base rates escapes the trade-off.
Conflates the three fairness families (demographic parity/independence, equalized odds/separation, calibration/sufficiency) or uses the terms interchangeably.
Recommends group-specific (race-conditional) thresholds as the fix without acknowledging the disparate-treatment / fair-lending (ECOA/Reg B) legal problem.
Picks a fairness criterion by fiat ('use equalized odds') without justifying it via the specific harms and error costs of this lending context.
Assumes the 'default' label is clean ground truth, ignoring that a biased target makes metric-equalization entrench rather than remove harm.
reference_answer:
This is the classic fairness-impossibility situation, not a bug. Three families of group-fairness criteria are in play: independence / demographic parity (equal approval rate), separation / equalized odds (equal TPR and FPR across groups), and sufficiency / calibration (a score means the same default probability in each group; the stronger form is equal PPV / predictive parity). The audit found calibration holds while FPR differs -- and given unequal base rates, those two facts are mutually consistent and mathematically forced.

Why: for a group with prevalence p, the confusion-matrix rates are tied together by
FPR = (p/(1-p)) . ((1-PPV)/PPV) . (1-FNR).
If you hold PPV (calibration/predictive parity) and FNR equal across groups but p differs, FPR must differ. Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan and Chouldechova prove the general result: calibration and equalized odds (balance for both classes) cannot both hold unless the classifier is perfect or the base rates are equal. So 'retrain until both are satisfied' is impossible short of a perfect model; more data or threshold tuning only slides you along the trade-off curve, it does not remove it.

What to actually do:
1. Treat it as a value decision, not metric optimization: choose the governing criterion by the dominant harm. Here the salient harm is denying credit to applicants who would have repaid (false positives on the 'good' outcome), which argues for prioritizing error-rate balance (equalized odds) even at some calibration cost -- and documenting that choice.
2. Post-processing (Hardt-Price-Srebro) can equalize odds via group-specific thresholds/randomization, but in US lending, race-conditional thresholds raise disparate-treatment concerns under ECOA / Regulation B, so flag the legal tension rather than shipping it blindly; weigh group-blind levers (better features, a reject-option review band).
3. Interrogate the label: 'default' may be a biased proxy (measurement/label bias, differential access to forbearance), so equalizing metrics on a biased target can entrench harm -- investigate target and data quality.
4. Evaluate rigorously: report subgroup and intersectional metrics with confidence intervals and adequate sample sizes, and monitor under distribution shift over time, not on one snapshot.
5. Communicate transparently that no model is 'fair' in the absolute -- the organization is selecting an explicit fairness definition and accepting a stated trade-off.
